content: Acupuncture is being increasingly utilized as a treatment option for individuals with epilepsy. However, the robustness of the existing evidence supporting its efficacy and safety remains uncertain. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of acupuncture in managing epilepsy. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and AMED, covering studies from their inception to June 2013. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing acupuncture with placebo, sham treatment, antiepileptic drugs, or no treatment, as well as acupuncture combined with other treatments, were included. No language restrictions were applied. Seventeen RCTs involving 1,538 participants with a wide age range and predominantly generalized epilepsy were included. The treatment duration varied from 7.5 weeks to 1 year. All trials were found to have a high risk of bias and short follow-up periods. When comparing needle acupuncture combined with Chinese herbs to Chinese herbs alone, no significant reduction in seizure frequency was observed (80% in the control group vs. 90% in the intervention group; relative risk [RR] 1.13, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.97 to 1.31). Similarly, needle acupuncture combined with valproate did not achieve seizure freedom (44% in the control group vs. 42.7% in the intervention group; RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.30) or a significant reduction in seizure frequency (69.3% in the control group vs. 81.3% in the intervention group; RR 1.34, 95% CI 0.52 to 3.48). However, it may have improved quality of life (QOL), as measured by the QOLIE-31 score (mean difference [MD] 10.10 points, 95% CI 2.51 to 17.69). When compared to phenytoin, needle acupuncture did not significantly reduce seizure frequency (70% in the control group vs. 94.4% in the intervention group; RR 1.43, 95% CI 0.46 to 4.44). Similarly, needle acupuncture alone compared to valproate did not achieve seizure freedom (14.1% in the control group vs. 25.2% in the intervention group; RR 1.75, 95% CI 0.93 to 3.27). However, it may have been effective in reducing seizure frequency by at least 50% (55.3% in the control group vs. 73.7% in the intervention group; RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.66) and improving QOL (MD 12.04 points, 95% CI 4.05 to 20.03). Catgut implantation at acupoints combined with antiepileptic drugs did not achieve seizure freedom compared to antiepileptic drugs alone (13% in the control group vs. 19.6% in the intervention group; RR 1.51, 95% CI 0.93 to 2.43). However, it may have been effective in reducing seizure frequency by at least 50% (63.1% in the control group vs. 82% in the intervention group; RR 1.42, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.89) and improving QOL (MD -7.54 points, 95% CI -14.47 to -0.61, where a lower score indicated better QOL). When compared to valproate, catgut implantation may have been effective in achieving seizure freedom (8% in the control group vs. 19.7% in the intervention group; RR 2.82, 95% CI 1.61 to 4.94) and improving QOL (MD 18.73 points, 95% CI 11.10 to 26.36). However, it did not significantly reduce seizure frequency by at least 50% (65.6% in the control group vs. 91.7% in the intervention group; RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.84). Across the included trials, acupuncture did not result in a higher incidence of adverse events compared to control treatments. In conclusion, the available RCTs are small, heterogeneous, and carry a high risk of bias. The current evidence does not support the use of acupuncture as an effective treatment for epilepsy.
